questions.stem: Which sequence shows the path of air from the nose to the site of gas exchange?
options: Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli
Nasal cavity, larynx, pharynx, bronchi, trachea, alveoli, bronchioles
Pharynx, nasal cavity, trachea, larynx, bronchioles, bronchi, alveoli
Nasal cavity, pharynx, trachea, larynx, bronchioles, alveoli, bronchi
questions.explanation: Air passes through the nasal cavity and pharynx to the larynx, then down the trachea, which branches into bronchi and then bronchioles ending in alveoli. The pharynx comes before the larynx.

questions.stem: Why does the trachea have C-shaped rings of cartilage in its wall?
options: They are the site where oxygen first enters the blood capillaries
They hold the airway open so it does not collapse when air pressure falls
They contract and relax to push air into and out of the lungs
They trap dust and microbes before these can reach the alveoli deep in the lungs
questions.explanation: Cartilage rings keep the trachea open as pressure inside it falls during inhalation. Trapping particles is the job of mucus and cilia, not cartilage.

questions.stem: The trachea is lined with ciliated epithelium containing goblet cells. How does this lining protect the lungs?
options: Goblet cells absorb dust particles and digest them inside lysosomes
Cilia beat to push the mucus and any trapped particles down into the alveoli
Mucus from goblet cells traps particles and cilia sweep it up to the throat
Cilia secrete enzymes that digest bacteria before they reach the bronchi
questions.explanation: Mucus traps dust and microbes and the beating cilia move it upwards to the pharynx, where it is swallowed. Moving it down into the alveoli would defeat the purpose.

questions.stem: Which changes occur during inhalation (inspiration)?
options: Diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards; internal intercostals pull the ribs down
Diaphragm contracts and domes upwards; intercostals pull the ribs down and in
Diaphragm relaxes and flattens; the ribs move up and out
Diaphragm contracts and flattens; external intercostals lift the ribs
questions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles enlarges the thoracic cavity. A diaphragm doming upwards is what happens as it relaxes during exhalation.

questions.stem: Why does air flow into the lungs when the thoracic cavity enlarges?
options: The pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure
The pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure
The lungs actively suck air in using their own muscle tissue
Oxygen diffuses in because the lungs contain less oxygen
questions.explanation: A larger volume lowers the pressure in the lungs, so air moves in from the higher atmospheric pressure outside. The lungs have no skeletal muscle of their own; they follow the chest wall.

questions.stem: Which feature of the alveolar wall best suits it to its role in the lungs?
options: A dry lining that stops oxygen dissolving
A small total surface area that limits water loss
Walls one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance
Thick muscular walls that pump air in and out
questions.explanation: Thin walls of simple squamous epithelium, close to equally thin capillaries, mean gases diffuse only a tiny distance. Alveoli have a huge total area and a moist lining in which gases dissolve.

questions.stem: How do breathing and blood flow together keep oxygen diffusing into the blood at the alveoli?
options: Breathing removes carbon dioxide from the blood and blood flow adds oxygen to the air
Breathing pushes oxygen through the walls and blood flow pulls it into the plasma
Breathing warms the air and blood flow slows down so the blood can pick up more
Breathing keeps alveolar oxygen high and blood flow carries oxygenated blood away
questions.explanation: Ventilation brings in fresh air, keeping oxygen high in the alveoli, while circulation constantly replaces oxygenated blood with deoxygenated blood. Together they maintain a steep concentration gradient.

questions.stem: Why is the inner surface of the alveoli moist?
options: The moisture traps any dust that has got past the cilia of the upper airways
Gases must dissolve in water before they diffuse across the alveolar wall
Water is needed to carry oxygen to the cells in the form of carbonic acid
The moisture is actively pumped in to cool the blood in the capillaries
questions.explanation: Oxygen dissolves in the thin film of fluid lining the alveoli before diffusing into the blood. A surfactant in this film also lowers surface tension so the alveoli do not collapse.

questions.stem: Long-term smoking destroys the walls between many alveoli, leaving fewer, larger air spaces. Why is the person short of breath?
options: The airways become wider, so air moves too quickly
The diffusion distance into the capillaries is reduced
The blood carries more carbon monoxide than oxygen at rest
The surface area for gas exchange is greatly reduced
questions.explanation: Fewer, larger air spaces have much less total surface area, so less oxygen can diffuse into the blood in each breath. This disease is emphysema, a long-term consequence of smoking.

questions.stem: Carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke binds strongly to haemoglobin. What is the short-term effect?
options: Blood clots more slowly after a cut or injury
More oxygen is released to the respiring cells
Red blood cells carry less oxygen to body tissues
Alveoli become thicker and gas exchange slows
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide occupies haemoglobin's binding sites, so less oxygen is carried; the heart must then work harder to meet demand. Thickened airways come from long-term irritation, not carbon monoxide.

questions.stem: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta?
options: Right ventricle
Left atrium
Right atrium
Left ventricle
questions.explanation: Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium, passes to the left ventricle and is pumped into the aorta. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

questions.stem: Why is the wall of the left ventricle much thicker than that of the right ventricle?
options: It pumps blood to the lungs, which resist flow more than the body
It needs extra muscle because it receives only deoxygenated blood
It must generate higher pressure to pump blood around the body
It must hold a larger volume of blood than the right ventricle
questions.explanation: The systemic circuit is long and high in resistance, so the left ventricle develops much higher pressure. Both ventricles pump the same volume per beat.

questions.stem: Which sequence traces blood returning from the body through the heart and lungs?
options: Vena cava, right ventricle, right atrium, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium
Vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium
Vena cava, left atrium, left ventricle, pulmonary vein, lungs, pulmonary artery, right atrium
Aorta, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary vein, lungs, pulmonary artery, left atrium
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the venae cavae, goes to the right ventricle and out through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, returning via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

questions.stem: What is the function of the bicuspid (mitral) and tricuspid valves?
options: They stop blood flowing back from the ventricles into the atria
They stop blood flowing back from the arteries into the ventricles
They control the rate at which the heart beats
They separate oxygenated from deoxygenated blood in the atria
questions.explanation: The atrioventricular valves close when the ventricles contract, preventing backflow into the atria. Backflow from the arteries is prevented by the semilunar valves.

questions.stem: In a tissue section, vessel X has a thick wall with much elastic and smooth muscle tissue and a small round lumen. Vessel Y has a thinner wall, a large irregular lumen and valves. Which identification is correct?
options: X is a capillary and Y is an artery
X is an artery and Y is a capillary
X is an artery and Y is a vein
X is a vein and Y is an artery
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood at high pressure, so they need thick elastic, muscular walls. Veins carry low-pressure blood, have wide lumens and contain valves; capillaries are a single cell layer thick.

questions.stem: How does the structure of capillaries suit their role in exchange with cells?
options: Wide lumens let blood flow fast so that more material is delivered
Walls one cell thick let materials pass quickly between blood and tissue fluid
Thick muscular walls push materials out of the blood into the cells
Valves all along their length direct materials into the surrounding body cells
questions.explanation: Capillary walls are a single layer of flattened endothelial cells, giving a short path for diffusion. Blood actually flows slowly through capillaries, allowing more time for exchange.

questions.stem: How is blood in the leg veins returned to the heart against gravity?
options: Contracting skeletal muscles squeeze the veins and valves stop backflow
The muscular walls of the veins pump the blood upwards in waves
The left ventricle generates enough pressure to push it all the way back
The capillaries in the legs pump blood actively into the veins
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle contractions compress the veins, and one-way valves ensure the blood moves only towards the heart. By the time blood reaches the veins, most of the pressure from the ventricle has been lost.

questions.stem: Blood leaving the small intestine after a meal is high in glucose and amino acids, yet blood leaving the liver has much less of them. Which vessel carries blood from the intestine to the liver?
options: Hepatic vein
Renal artery
Hepatic portal vein
Hepatic artery
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut directly to the liver, which stores and processes the nutrients. The hepatic vein carries blood from the liver to the vena cava.

questions.stem: In which form is most oxygen carried in the blood?
options: Erythrocytes, bound to haemoglobin
Plasma, dissolved in water
Leucocytes, bound to antibodies
Platelets, bound to fibrinogen
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells (erythrocytes) carries most of the oxygen. Very little oxygen dissolves in plasma.

questions.stem: Which materials are transported dissolved in blood plasma?
options: Only water and salts, because all of the other materials are carried inside blood cells
Glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones and most carbon dioxide (as hydrogen carbonate)
Oxygen bound to haemoglobin, platelets and white blood cells
Starch, proteins from food and fats in large undigested droplets
questions.explanation: Plasma is mostly water carrying dissolved nutrients, wastes, hormones, plasma proteins and most carbon dioxide as hydrogen carbonate ions. Oxygen travels mainly in red blood cells.

questions.stem: How do the biconcave shape and lack of a nucleus help an erythrocyte do its job?
options: They give a large surface area and more room for haemoglobin
They let the cell divide quickly to replace damaged red cells
They let the cell engulf bacteria in the blood by phagocytosis
They give the cell more mitochondria to use the oxygen it carries
questions.explanation: The biconcave disc increases surface area for gas exchange and the space freed by losing the nucleus is filled with haemoglobin. Mature red blood cells have no mitochondria either, so they do not use the oxygen they carry.

questions.stem: What is the main role of leucocytes?
options: Carrying hormones to target organs
Defending the body against pathogens
Carrying oxygen to respiring cells
Forming a plug and starting clotting
questions.explanation: White blood cells (leucocytes) protect the body: some engulf pathogens by phagocytosis and lymphocytes produce antibodies. Clotting is started by platelets.

questions.stem: In blood clotting, which conversion forms the mesh of threads that traps blood cells?
options: Fibrinogen to fibrin, catalysed by thrombin
Fibrin to fibrinogen, catalysed by prothrombin
Prothrombin to fibrinogen, catalysed by calcium
Thrombin to prothrombin, catalysed by fibrin
questions.explanation: Damaged tissue and platelets release factors that convert prothrombin to thrombin, using calcium ions, and thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads. The reverse conversions do not occur.

questions.stem: A patient's full blood count shows far fewer platelets than normal. Which problem would you expect them to report?
options: Frequent infections because pathogens are not engulfed
Swelling of the legs because tissue fluid is not drained
Bruising easily and bleeding for longer from small cuts
Tiredness from a reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
questions.explanation: Platelets form plugs and trigger clotting, so too few means prolonged bleeding and bruising. Tiredness from low oxygen-carrying capacity would point to anaemia instead.

questions.stem: What are the two main functions of the lymphatic system?
options: Carrying oxygen to tissues and removing carbon dioxide from them
Returning tissue fluid to the blood and helping protect against disease
Pumping blood to the lungs and filtering urea from the blood
Producing digestive enzymes and absorbing water from the colon
questions.explanation: Lymph vessels collect excess tissue fluid and return it to the bloodstream, and lymph nodes filter it and house lymphocytes. The kidneys, not lymph, filter urea from blood.

questions.stem: How does tissue fluid form at a capillary bed?
options: Red blood cells burst in the capillaries and release their contents into the tissues
Lymph vessels pump fluid out into the spaces between the cells of the tissue
Cells secrete water and salts by exocytosis into the spaces around them
Blood pressure forces plasma, without large proteins or cells, out through the capillary walls
questions.explanation: At the arterial end of a capillary, blood pressure pushes water and small solutes out to bathe the cells. Most is reabsorbed and the excess drains into lymph capillaries.

questions.stem: Where does lymph rejoin the blood?
options: In the alveoli of the lungs
In large veins near the heart, under the collarbones
In the arteries leaving the left ventricle
In the capillaries of every tissue in the body
questions.explanation: Lymph drains through lymph vessels to the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct, which empty into the subclavian veins near the heart. Lymph does not enter arteries.

questions.stem: Lymph nodes in a person's neck become swollen and tender during a throat infection. What is the best explanation?
options: Lymph vessels have become blocked, so tissue fluid is building up in the neck
The nodes are producing extra red blood cells to replace those the infection destroyed
Bacteria have damaged the nodes so that they cannot filter lymph any longer
Lymphocytes are multiplying in the nodes to fight the pathogens filtered from lymph
questions.explanation: Lymph nodes filter pathogens from lymph and contain lymphocytes, which multiply during infection, enlarging the node. Swelling here signals an active immune response rather than a blockage.

questions.stem: Where in the small intestine are digested fats absorbed into the lymphatic system?
options: The hepatic portal vein
Lacteals in the villi
Capillaries in the villi
Lymph nodes in the gut wall
questions.explanation: Each villus contains a lacteal, a lymph capillary that takes up absorbed fats. Glucose and amino acids enter the blood capillaries instead.

questions.stem: A person has blood group A. Which antigens are on their red blood cells and which antibodies are in their plasma?
options: A antigens; anti-B antibodies
A antigens; anti-A antibodies
B antigens; anti-A antibodies
No antigens; anti-A and anti-B antibodies
questions.explanation: Group A red cells carry A antigens, and the plasma contains anti-B antibodies. Having anti-A antibodies would make the person's own cells clump.

questions.stem: Why is group O Rhesus negative red cell blood often given in an emergency when the patient's group is unknown?
options: Its red cells carry every antigen, so they match all possible recipients' red cells
It contains extra clotting factors that stop bleeding in trauma patients quickly
Its red cells lack A, B and D antigens, so the recipient's antibodies cannot bind them
Its plasma has no antibodies, so it cannot react with any recipient's red blood cells
questions.explanation: Without A, B or Rhesus D antigens, the donor red cells have nothing for the recipient's antibodies to attack. Group O plasma actually contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

questions.stem: A patient with group B blood is mistakenly given group A red blood cells. What happens?
options: Nothing happens, because A and B are co-dominant and so are compatible
The patient's B antigens are converted into A antigens by the donor cells
The patient's anti-A antibodies agglutinate the donor cells, causing a transfusion reaction
The donor's anti-B antibodies destroy all of the patient's own red cells straight away
questions.explanation: A group B person has anti-A antibodies, which bind to the A antigens on the donated cells and make them clump and break down. This blocks small vessels and can be fatal, which is why blood is cross-matched.

questions.stem: Which person can safely receive red blood cells from a donor of any ABO and Rhesus group?
options: AB Rhesus negative
O Rhesus positive
AB Rhesus positive
O Rhesus negative
questions.explanation: An AB positive person has A, B and D antigens and so makes no anti-A, anti-B or anti-D antibodies to attack donor cells. O negative is the universal red cell donor, not recipient.

questions.stem: A Rhesus negative person receives Rhesus positive blood for the first time and has no immediate reaction. Why might a second such transfusion be dangerous?
options: Rhesus negative people are born with anti-D antibodies that build up over many years
The donor cells from the first transfusion stay in the blood and attack new donor cells
Rhesus antigens accumulate in the liver and cause it to fail after the second transfusion
The first transfusion caused them to make anti-D antibodies that will attack the cells
questions.explanation: Rhesus negative people do not naturally carry anti-D antibodies but can make them after exposure to Rhesus positive cells. A later exposure then triggers a strong antibody response against the donated cells.

questions.stem: Donated blood is often separated into red cells, plasma and platelets. What is the main advantage?
options: Each component can treat a different patient's specific condition
Separating the components removes the need to test the blood group
Whole blood cannot be stored at all, even for a few hours
Separation destroys any pathogens that the donor's blood carries
questions.explanation: Red cells can treat anaemia or blood loss, platelets help people with clotting problems, and plasma products help burns and clotting factor deficiencies, so one donation helps several people. Blood groups must still be checked.

questions.stem: A person's coronary arteries are narrowed by fatty plaques, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. How does inserting a stent treat this?
options: A drug inside the stent dissolves the heart muscle damaged by the reduced blood flow
A new valve replaces the faulty valve that allowed the plaque to build up in the artery
A mesh tube holds the narrowed artery open so blood flows freely to the heart muscle
A small pump attached to the artery pushes blood past the blockage into the ventricle
questions.explanation: A stent is a small mesh tube expanded inside the artery to keep it open, restoring blood supply to the heart muscle. It treats the narrowed vessel; valves are a separate structure.

questions.stem: Which lifestyle change would most help reduce a person's risk of atherosclerosis?
options: Replacing water with sugary drinks
Stopping smoking and exercising regularly
Increasing intake of saturated fats
Spending more of each day sitting down
questions.explanation: Smoking damages artery linings and inactivity raises blood pressure and cholesterol, both promoting fatty plaques. Regular exercise and not smoking lower the risk.
